meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Change happens at the speed of trust'?
meta.ogDescription: Two Coveys, one phrase. Wikiquote calls this sentence disputed; the 2006 book it gets credited to words it differently.

answer.label: Not Stephen R. Covey — a reworded slogan from his son's book
answer.authorDates: American author · former President and CEO of the Covey Leadership Center · wrote The SPEED of Trust (2006)
answer.sourceLine: “The speed of trust” is Stephen M. R. Covey’s phrase, from The SPEED of Trust: The One Thing That Changes Everything (Free Press, 2006) — not his father Stephen R. Covey, the 7 Habits author most people mean when they say “Stephen Covey.” But we could not document this exact sentence in that book or in any Covey interview: Wikiquote lists it as disputed ↗, and the wording Covey actually uses is “Nothing is as fast as the speed of trust.”

source.excerpt: Nothing is as fast as the speed of trust.
trail: Wikiquote’s Stephen Covey page ↗ prints the line in a Disputed subsection as “Change happens at the speed of trust. (cf. The SPEED of Trust, 2008)” — a comparison, not a citation. (Wikiquote’s parenthesis says 2008; the book itself first appeared in 2006.)

The book that phrase points to is not the father’s. Open Library ↗ records The SPEED of Trust as first published in 2006 by Free Press, by Stephen M. R. Covey with Rebecca R. Merrill, and Wikipedia ↗ notes that Stephen R. Covey (1932–2012) supplied its foreword.
The book’s own formulation differs. The November 2006 Soundview digest ↗ heads its opening section “Nothing Is as Fast as the Speed of Trust,” and contains no sentence beginning “Change happens.”

Covey said that version aloud too: in DC Velocity, April 2008 issue ↗, he put it as “once you have established the trust, nothing is as fast as the speed of trust.” The reader-compiled Goodreads quote list for the book ↗ carries the popular sentence nowhere either.
source.excerptNote: This is the formulation the book actually runs on: it is the opening section heading of the November 2006 Soundview digest ↗ of The SPEED of Trust, and Covey used the same words himself in a 2008 interview ↗. The popular sentence — “Change happens at the speed of trust” — appears in neither.

source.rightsNote: No first publication can be tied to this exact sentence, so no rights status can honestly be claimed for it. The nearest documented wording sits in The SPEED of Trust, first published in 2006 by Free Press per Open Library ↗ — comfortably in copyright — so treat any extended quotation from that book as protected.

author.name: Stephen M. R. Covey
author.heading: Whose phrase it actually is
author.metaLine: American author · former President and CEO of the Covey Leadership Center · The SPEED of Trust (2006)
author.bio: Stephen M. R. Covey is the eldest son of 7 Habits author Stephen R. Covey, and led the family firm before merging it with Franklin Quest to create FranklinCovey. His own book, The SPEED of Trust (Free Press, 2006, written with Rebecca R. Merrill and carrying a foreword by his father), argued that trust is a measurable economic asset: where it is high, work moves faster and costs less. FranklinCovey ↗ describes him as the former President and CEO of the Covey Leadership Center and the leader of its Global Speed of Trust Practice.

copyAttribution: "Change happens at the speed of trust." — commonly credited to Stephen Covey, but Wikiquote lists the sentence as disputed. "The speed of trust" is his son Stephen M. R. Covey's phrase, from The SPEED of Trust (New York: Free Press, 2006); the wording Covey himself uses, and the wording the book's contemporary Soundview digest heads its opening section with, is "Nothing is as fast as the speed of trust."

misattribution.heading: Where the credit goes wrong
misattribution.intro: “Stephen Covey” is two people, and this line gets pinned on the wrong one — then quoted as if it came out of a book that words it differently.

items.why: The 7 Habits author is who most readers mean by “Stephen Covey,” and quote sites file the line under him: QuotePark ↗ credits Stephen R. Covey — and files it under his First Things First (1994) — while the line itself points at The SPEED of Trust. That entry is a Wikiquote mirror, marked “Disputed” and labelled “Adopted from Wikiquote,” so it shows how the credit travels rather than adding independent evidence for it. Wikipedia ↗ records that the 2006 trust book was written by his son Stephen M. R. Covey with Rebecca Merrill; the father supplied only the foreword.

The idea is his, but the sentence is a compression. The November 2006 Soundview digest of the book ↗ heads its opening section “Nothing Is as Fast as the Speed of Trust,” and the reader-compiled Goodreads quote list for the book ↗ carries no “Change happens” line.
Emergent Strategy’s core principles include “Move at the speed of trust” ↗ — a separate organizing maxim that often gets merged with the Covey slogan in the same slide deck.

Bailey’s much-repeated pairing is “Social change happens at the speed of relationships. And relationships move at the speed of trust,” as quoted by the Einhorn Collaborative ↗ — close enough to be mistaken for the slogan, but not the same sentence.

misattribution.truthLine: The thinking is Stephen M. R. Covey’s; the sentence is nobody’s in particular. Wikiquote lists it as disputed ↗, and no Covey book digest, interview or quote collection we fetched uses this wording.

context.heading: Why this one travels
lead: The thesis is real and it is Stephen M. R. Covey’s: trust is not a soft virtue but a hard economic variable, and where it is high, work moves faster and costs less. What travels on conference slides is not that argument — it is a seven-word compression of it, with the author’s name shortened to “Stephen Covey,” which is where the trouble starts.

“Stephen Covey” is two people. The father, Stephen R. Covey, wrote The 7 Habits of Highly Effective People; the son, Stephen M. R. Covey, wrote The SPEED of Trust and contributed the foreword the other way round. Quote sites resolve the ambiguity toward the more famous name, so a line derived from the son’s book ends up filed under the father — and then quoted in a wording neither man is documented using.
context.detailsSummary: What the digest and the interview say
detailsBody: The November 2006 Soundview Executive Book Summaries digest ↗ of The SPEED of Trust opens with the section heading “Nothing Is as Fast as the Speed of Trust.” That heading is the digest editors’ summary of the argument rather than a line lifted from the book, but Covey used the same words out loud: asked about it by DC Velocity in its April 2008 issue ↗, he said that “once you have established the trust, nothing is as fast as the speed of trust.”

Two adjacent maxims circulate in organizing and civic-trust circles and get blended with the Covey line: adrienne maree brown’s Emergent Strategy principle “Move at the speed of trust” ↗, and Rev. Jennifer Bailey’s pairing of relationships and social change. Neither is the sentence on the slide, and neither claims to be.
context.pull: Two Coveys, one phrase — and a sentence neither of them is documented saying.

sourcesVerified.claim: Wikiquote prints "Change happens at the speed of trust. (cf. The SPEED of Trust, 2008)" in a Disputed subsection of its Stephen Covey page.
Stephen R. Covey lived 1932-2012, wrote The 7 Habits, and his son Stephen M. R. Covey wrote The Speed of Trust (2006) with Rebecca Merrill, with a foreword by Stephen R. Covey.

The November 2006 Soundview Executive Book Summaries digest (vol. 28, no. 11) of The SPEED of Trust heads its opening section "Nothing Is as Fast as the Speed of Trust" and contains no "change happens" sentence.

In a DC Velocity interview dated 1 April 2008, Stephen M. R. Covey said "once you have established the trust, nothing is as fast as the speed of trust", and did not use the phrase "change happens at the speed of trust".
Open Library records The SPEED of Trust: The One Thing that Changes Everything by Stephen M. R. Covey and Rebecca R. Merrill, first published 2006, publisher Free Press.
FranklinCovey describes Stephen M. R. Covey as the former President and CEO of the Covey Leadership Center who co-founded and leads FranklinCovey's Global Speed of Trust Practice.
Goodreads' reader-compiled quote pages for The Speed of Trust do not include "Change happens at the speed of trust" or "change moves at the speed of trust".
QuotePark credits "Change happens at the speed of trust. (cf. The SPEED of Trust, 2008)" to Stephen R. Covey, marked Disputed and adopted from Wikiquote.
The Einhorn Collaborative quotes Rev. Jen Bailey of the Faith Matters Network: "Social change happens at the speed of relationships. And relationships move at the speed of trust."
